PAGE 1

5.3 Solution Curves / Phase Portraits

Summary of \(\vec{x}' = A\vec{x}\): Real and Distinct Eigenvalues

Case 1: Both Eigenvalues Negative (\(\lambda_1, \lambda_2 < 0\))

System Definition & Straight Line Solutions:

\[ \vec{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & \sqrt{2} \\ \sqrt{2} & -2 \end{bmatrix}\vec{x} \] \[ \lambda_1 = -1, \quad \vec{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ \sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix}; \qquad \lambda_2 = -4, \quad \vec{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -\sqrt{2} \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

Note: Eigenvectors define straight-line solution trajectories in the phase plane.

Concept Note: For any 2D linear system \(\vec{x}' = A\vec{x}\) with real eigenvalues, the general solution is \(\vec{x}(t) = c_1 e^{\lambda_1 t}\vec{v}_1 + c_2 e^{\lambda_2 t}\vec{v}_2\). When one constant is zero, trajectories are straight lines along the eigenvector axes pointing toward (or away from) the origin.

Asymptotic Behavior & Classification

  • Behavior at \(t \to \infty\):

    As \(t \to \infty\), \(e^{\lambda t} \to 0\) because both \(\lambda < 0\). Therefore, all trajectories approach the origin \(\vec{x}=\vec{0}\).

  • Dominant Eigenvector Direction:

    Since \(|-1| < |-4|\), \(e^{-4t}\) decays much faster than \(e^{-t}\) (i.e., \(e^{-t}> e^{-4t}\) as \(t \to \infty\)).

    Near the origin, solution curves become tangent to and follow the eigenvector corresponding to \(\lambda = -1\), namely \(\vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ \sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix}\).

  • Equilibrium Classification:

    The origin is an improper nodal sink (stable node):

    • Improper: Trajectories enter the origin tangent to a single line (asymptote).
    • Nodal: Non-spiral point equilibrium.
    • Sink: All solutions flow into the origin as \(t \to \infty\).
PAGE 2

Case 2: Both Eigenvalues Positive (\(\lambda_1, \lambda_2 > 0\))

System Definition & Straight Line Solutions:

\[ \vec{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -1 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\vec{x} \] \[ \lambda_1 = 2, \quad \vec{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}; \qquad \lambda_2 = 4, \quad \vec{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

Concept Note: When all eigenvalues are positive, the origin is unstable. Trajectories flow outward toward infinity as \(t \to \infty\). Conversely, tracing backward in time (\(t \to -\infty\)), trajectories emerge from the origin tangent to the slower growth eigenvector (smallest positive eigenvalue).

Asymptotic Behavior & Classification

  • Behavior as \(t \to -\infty\) (Near Origin):

    As \(t \to -\infty\), \(e^{2t} > e^{4t}\) (since \(e^{4t}\) vanishes much faster). The term with the smaller eigenvalue \(\lambda = 2\) dominates near the origin.

  • Exit Direction:

    All solution trajectories leave the origin along/tangent to \(\vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}\) corresponding to \(\lambda = 2\).

  • Equilibrium Classification:

    The origin is an improper nodal source (unstable node).

PAGE 3

\(\lambda\)'s Real and Opposite in Signs

Linear System:

\[ \vec{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \vec{x} \]

Eigenvalues: \(\lambda = 3, \; -1\)

Eigenvectors: \(\vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}, \; \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}\)

Classification Note

When the real eigenvalues have opposite signs (\(\lambda_1 > 0\) and \(\lambda_2 < 0\)), the equilibrium point at the origin is always an unstable saddle point. Trajectories approach the origin along the stable eigenspace (\(\lambda = -1\)) and diverge along the unstable eigenspace (\(\lambda = 3\)).

Origin is a saddle point

PAGE 4

\(\lambda\)'s are Repeated

Linear System:

\[ \vec{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \vec{x} \]

Eigenvalues: \(\lambda = 1, \; 1\)

Eigenvectors: \(\vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \; \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\)

(matrix is complete \(\rightarrow\) not defective)

Key Concept: Star Node

Because the matrix is a scalar multiple of the identity \(I\), every non-zero vector in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue \(\lambda = 1\). Therefore, every trajectory is a straight ray emanating directly away from the origin.

Eigenvalues are equal, so neither eigenvector is more important \(\rightarrow\) solutions are linear combos of both.

Origin is sometimes called a “star node” and is a proper nodal source.

\(\rightarrow\) no preferred asymptote

PAGE 5

Repeated Eigenvalues: Defective Case (Improper Nodal Sink)

\[ \vec{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -4 \\ 4 & -7 \end{bmatrix} \vec{x} \]

The characteristic equation is \(\det(A - \lambda I) = (1-\lambda)(-7-\lambda) + 16 = \lambda^2 + 6\lambda + 9 = (\lambda + 3)^2 = 0\), yielding a repeated eigenvalue \(\lambda = -3\) of algebraic multiplicity 2.

\[ \lambda = -3, -3 \] \[ \vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad \text{defect of one} \]

Solving \((A - (-3)I)\vec{v} = \mathbf{0}\) gives \(4v_1 - 4v_2 = 0 \implies v_1 = v_2\). Since there is only one linearly independent eigenvector for a multiplicity 2 eigenvalue, the matrix has a geometric multiplicity of 1 and an eigenvalue defect of 1.

One straight line solution visible.

Origin is improper nodal sink

Because the repeated eigenvalue is strictly negative (\(\lambda = -3 < 0\)), all trajectories flow asymptotically into the origin as \(t \to \infty\), entering tangentially along the span of the single eigenvector \(\vec{v}=[1, 1]^T\).
PAGE 6

Complex \(\lambda\)'s

\[ \vec{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -5 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \vec{x} \]

\[ \lambda = i, -i \] \[ \vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 2+i \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \; \begin{bmatrix} 2-i \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

\(\lambda\)'s are purely imaginary, so solution curves are ovals.

Orientation? * Incomplete see next page
When the eigenvalues are purely imaginary (\(\text{Re}(\lambda) = 0\)), the solutions are periodic sines and cosines, resulting in concentric closed elliptical orbits (ovals) centered at the origin.
PAGE 7

Ellipse Orientation

Eigenvectors: \[ \vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + i \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \; \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} - i \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \]

For a linear dynamical system with purely imaginary or complex conjugate eigenvalues, the phase trajectories form ellipses. The real and imaginary vector components of the eigenvector \( \vec{v} = \vec{u} \pm i\vec{w} \) span the conjugate axes that determine the orientation and tilt of the trajectory.

Form a parallelogram with \( \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \pm \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \)

Ellipse is inside the parallelogram

The elliptical orbit is inscribed within and tangent to the parallelogram spanned by the vectors \( \pm \vec{u} \) and \( \pm \vec{w} \), where \( \vec{u} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \) and \( \vec{w} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \).

PAGE 8

Complex Eigenvalues with Non-Zero Real Part

If real part of \( \lambda \) is not zero, then the ovals grow or shrink as they go around.

Linear System

\[ \vec{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 5 & -3 \end{bmatrix} \vec{x} \]

Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors

\[ \lambda = -1 + i, \; -1 - i \] \[ \vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 + i \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}, \; \begin{bmatrix} 2 - i \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} \]

The general solution takes the form \( \vec{x}(t) = e^{\alpha t} (c_1 \cos(\beta t) + c_2 \sin(\beta t)) \vec{v}_r + \dots \) where \( \lambda = \alpha \pm i\beta \). The factor \( e^{\alpha t} = e^{-t} \) modulates the amplitude over time.

Figure out orientation and direction as before.

Here, real part of \( \lambda \) is negative, so “oval” shrinks as they go.

Origin is a spiral sink

Because \( \text{Re}(\lambda) = -1 < 0 \), the state asymptotically decays to zero \( \lim_{t \to \infty} \vec{x}(t)=\vec{0} \), forming a stable spiral sink (focus).

PAGE 9

An Unusual Case: One Eigenvalue is Zero

System Equations and General Solution

System Matrix

\[ \vec{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \vec{x} \]

Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors

\[ \lambda = 0, \; 5 \]\[ \vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \; \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \]

General Solution

\[ \vec{x} = c_1 \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + c_2 e^{5t} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \]
Conceptual Note: When an eigenvalue is zero (\(\lambda_1 = 0\)), the exponential factor \(e^{0t} = 1\) remains constant over time. Hence, any scalar multiple \(c_1 \vec{v}_1\) forms a stationary equilibrium point.

Phase Portrait Analysis

Equilibrium Line (\(\lambda = 0\))

Along the eigenvector \(\begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\):

  • Every point on this line is an equilibrium (\(\vec{x}' = \vec{0}\)).
  • No directions / zero velocity vectors along this line.

Trajectory Flow (\(\lambda = 5\))

Along the eigenvector direction \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\):

  • Because \(\lambda = 5 > 0\), trajectories flow directly outwards away from the line of equilibria.
  • All trajectories move in parallel straight lines along the direction of \(\vec{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\).
